newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Five more killed in Nigerian ethnic feud - papers.
newsitem.headline: Five more killed in Nigerian ethnic feud - papers.

text.p: Five more people have been killed in communal clashes in the oil-producing Warri area in midwestern Nigeria, newspapers reported on Wednesday.
Hostilities started on March 22 when clashes between armed youths broke out over a move of the local council headquarters from an Ijaw town to that of the rival Itsekiri tribe.
The death toll has risen to about 65 since April 12 when clashes resumed. A curfew imposed after the March clashes was lifted last week.

There was no police confirmation but the independent Guardian newspaper said the latest victims included a policeman, riot police had moved in to restore order, and soldiers might be sent in a last-ditch effort to restore peace.
The independent Punch reported that a policeman had been kidnapped by rioters and several women abducted.
State radio reported that the police had begun mass arrests of suspected rioters following the abductions.

Royal Dutch Shell Group's Nigerian unit, which pumps roughly half Nigeria's oil output of about two million barrels per day (bpd), said it had closed one flow station and output was running 2,000 bpd below normal.

A Shell spokeman told Reuters in Lagos that some of its oil exports from Nigeria, which had been stopped because of a strike by staff of a contractor that handles tanker berthing and loading, would resume on Wednesday afternoon after the strike was called off.

At the height of the crisis in March, armed Ijaw tribesmen occupied six Shell oil flow stations, shutting off a total of 100,000 bpd there. A total of 127 of Shell's Nigerian staff held hostage by the tribesmen were released in groups following negotiations and oil output has since resumed.
A navy ship was sent to Warri last weekend to ensure that oil production, Nigeria's economic backbone, was not affected.
